meta.ogDescription: Verified: Groucho's 1929 jacket blurb for S. J. Perelman's Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge. The familiar 'laid it down' version is a 1962 LIFE rewrite.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Groucho really wrote this — not as a stage ad-lib but as a paid-in-wit book blurb, printed in 1929 on the rear panel of the dust jacket of Dawn Ginsbergh’s Revenge, the first book by his future screenwriter S. J. Perelman. Quote Investigator ↗ traced it to the jacket itself and to a newspaper printing dated 7 October 1929, and the wording above is the 1929 wording.

source.excerpt: From the moment I picked up your book until I put it down, I was convulsed with laughter. Some day I intend reading it.
trail: 7 October 1929 — the earliest printing documented by Quote Investigator ↗: a “New Books Received by Greeley Library” column in The Greeley Daily Tribune of Greeley, Colorado, carrying the remark credited to Groucho Marx about Perelman’s new book.

1929 — the blurb sat on the rear panel of the Horace Liveright dust jacket, and dealers cataloguing jacketed 1929 copies still transcribe it off the jacket ↗. QI also cites a Google Books snippet of the jacket page and a 2010 American Dialect Society message from Fred Shapiro reporting the quote verified.
9 February 1962 — LIFE ran a close-up on Perelman with the verbs flipped, and that printing is the citation Wikiquote gives for the line ↗.
1989 — QI records that Leo Rosten’s Giant Book of Laughter put a reworded version on its back flap, re-aimed at a book of Rosten’s own ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the 1929 wording. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in the 7 October 1929 Greeley Daily Tribune library-acquisitions column and in a Google Books snippet of the book’s dust jacket. A dealer transcribing the jacket of a surviving 1929 copy — a third printing, issued the same month as the first — renders the closing sentence as “Someday I intend to read it” ↗ — the same joke, a hair of spacing and tense apart.

source.rightsNote: The blurb was first published in 1929 — on the dust jacket of Dawn Ginsbergh’s Revenge (Horace Liveright, New York) and in The Greeley Daily Tribune of 7 October 1929. United States works first published before 1931 are in the public domain, so the sentence itself is free to quote and reproduce. Note that the surrounding book text is Perelman’s, published the same year and likewise public domain.

author.name: Groucho Marx
author.heading: About Groucho Marx
author.bio: Julius Henry Marx — Groucho — was the greasepaint-moustached, cigar-waving centre of the Marx Brothers, working through vaudeville, Broadway, films, radio and television. He was also, by his own preference, a writer: he published essays in The New Yorker and the books Groucho and Me (1959), Memoirs of a Mangy Lover (1963) and The Groucho Letters (1967), and once said he would rather be remembered as a writer ↗ than as a comedian. This blurb is that side of him in one sentence: a joke built entirely out of syntax.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The wording usually isn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous Groucho lines he demonstrably wrote. What travels badly is the wording — and, in one case, which book he was talking about.

items.why: Its close-up on Perelman printed the quip with the verbs flipped — “picked your book up … laid it down” — and Quote Investigator notes that modern instances have altered the original wording ↗. That magazine printing is the citation Wikiquote attaches to the line ↗, which is why the flipped version is the one most people meet.

QI records ↗ that the 1989 printing (copyright 1985) carried the quip on its back flap applied to a book of Rosten’s own rather than Perelman’s, reworded to “I could not stop laughing. Some day I hope to read it.”

Most sites strip the blurb of its origin entirely. The Quotations Page ↗, for instance, runs a hybrid — “picked up your book … laid it down” — credited to Groucho with no book, no date and no publication named.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Groucho’s, and it has an address: the back of the dust jacket of S. J. Perelman’s first book, published by Horace Liveright in 1929, as traced by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: A blurb is supposed to say the book is good. Groucho’s says only that holding the book was hilarious, and then cheerfully admits he never opened it — and Horace Liveright printed it on the jacket anyway. That is the whole joke: the sentence is structured exactly like praise and delivers none.

The book it sat on was Dawn Ginsbergh’s Revenge, S. J. Perelman’s first, a collection of humorous pieces that Wikipedia describes as largely juvenilia ↗, many written while Perelman was a student at Brown. Perelman went on to write for the Marx Brothers on screen — a working relationship the same article records as a famously prickly one.
detailsBody: The version most people know is slightly different: “picked your book up … laid it down.” That flip came from a 1962 LIFE close-up on Perelman, and it is the version Wikiquote cites ↗. Both carry the same joke; only one is what the 1929 jacket said.

Surviving 1929 copies preserve the blurb. A dealer catalogue for a jacketed one transcribes it off the rear panel ↗, closing with “Someday I intend to read it” — a hair away from the “Some day I intend reading it” that the 1929 newspaper printing and the jacket snippet give.
context.pull: It reads like a rave right up to the last five words.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the quip was crafted by Groucho Marx and appeared in 1929 on the book jacket of Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge by S. J. Perelman; its earliest citation is the Greeley Daily Tribune, 7 October 1929, p.10, col.3, in a 'New Books Received by Greeley Library' item; it also cites a Google Books dust-jacket snippet, a Walter Winchell column (Scranton Republican, 20 Nov 1929), a 2010 American Dialect Society message from Fred Shapiro, LIFE of 9 February 1962 ('Close-up: S. J. Perelman – The Cranky Humorist', p.85) with altered wording, and Leo Rosten's Giant Book of Laughter (1989, copyright 1985) back flap re-aiming the quip at a Rosten book with the wording 'I could not stop laughing. Some day I hope to read it.'

Wikiquote's Groucho Marx page lists 'From the moment I picked your book up until I laid it down I was convulsed with laughter. Someday I intend on reading it.' under its Quotes section, noted as 'To S. J. Perelman about his book Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge (1929), as quoted in LIFE (9 February 1962)'.

Between the Covers Rare Books describes a 1929 Horace Liveright copy of Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge — explicitly a third printing, from the same month as the first printing and in the same green plush binding as the first issue, in a very good or better jacket — and transcribes the Groucho Marx blurb from the rear panel of the dust jacket: 'From the moment I picked up your book until I put it down I was convulsed with laughter. Someday I intend to read it.'
The Internet Archive hosts a full scan of S. J. Perelman's Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge (1929), his debut, described as long out of print with the pieces having first appeared in Judge magazine.

Wikipedia records S. J. Perelman (1 February 1904 – 17 October 1979) as an American humorist and screenwriter, lists Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge (1929) as largely juvenilia with many pieces written while he was a student at Brown, and covers his work on Marx Brothers films.

Wikipedia records Groucho Marx as Julius Henry Marx (2 October 1890 – 19 August 1977), an American comedian, actor, comic vocalist and game show host, author of Groucho and Me (1959), Memoirs of a Mangy Lover (1963) and The Groucho Letters (1967), who said he would prefer to be remembered as a writer and published essays in The New Yorker.

The Quotations Page prints 'From the moment I picked up your book until I laid it down, I was convulsed with laughter. Some day I intend reading it.' credited simply to 'Groucho Marx, US comedian with Marx Brothers (1890 - 1977)' with no source, book, date or publication cited.
Black Swan Books lists a first edition of Dawn Ginsbergh's Revenge published by Horace Liveright, New York, 1929, in the first-state apple green plush binding.
